q: Distinguish lexeme, lemma, sense and synset.
short: Lexeme: abstract dictionary entry (family of forms). Lemma: its citation form (run). Sense: one meaning of the lexeme (bank₁ finance). Synset: a set of synonyms expressing one concept, WordNet's node.
detail: One lemma, many senses; one synset, many lemmas.
mistakes: Calling lemma and sense the same.

q: Homonymy vs polysemy?
short: Homonymy: identical forms with unrelated meanings (bat animal/equipment). Polysemy: one word with related meanings sharing a core idea (paper: newspaper, exam paper).

q: Define hypernymy and meronymy with examples.
short: Hypernymy: is-a (vehicle is a hypernym of car; car of SUV). Meronymy: part-of (wheel is a meronym of car; finger of hand).
detail: Hyponym and holonym are the inverses.
mistakes: Calling wheel a hyponym of car.

q: What is WordNet?
short: A lexical database of English organising synsets (concepts) connected by semantic relations (hypernymy, meronymy, antonymy, entailment…), separately for nouns, verbs, adjectives and adverbs: a dictionary as a graph.
detail: Used for similarity, WSD, query expansion.
mistakes: Calling it a thesaurus of strings only.

q: What is word sense disambiguation?
short: Choosing which sense of an ambiguous word is meant in a particular context, e.g. bank in 'approved my loan' = financial institution.

q: Why is the most-frequent-sense baseline important?
short: It is cheap and often strong (sense distributions are skewed), so any WSD method must beat it to justify its cost; it fails on rare senses and on domains with different sense distributions.

q: How does Naive Bayes perform WSD?
short: Estimate P(sense) and P(context word | sense) from sense-tagged sentences (with smoothing), then choose argmax P(sense)·Π P(wᵢ | sense) for the observed context words.

q: Describe the Lesk algorithm.
short: For each candidate sense, count words shared between the target's context and the sense's dictionary gloss (ignoring stop words); choose the sense with maximum overlap.

q: Compute the Naive Bayes WSD scores for 'The bank approved my loan'.
Compute path similarity for bat (animal) vs dog and bat (animal) vs bat (cricket bat) in the mini hierarchy.
short: bat₁ → mammal ← dog: path 2 → 1/3. bat₁ → mammal → animal → entity ← artifact ← equipment ← bat₂: path 6 → 1/7.
mistakes: Treating both bats as one node.

q: Why does plain Lesk fail on 'The fisherman caught a bass'?
short: No literal overlap: 'fisherman' is not in the fish gloss (fish, sea, water) nor the music gloss; both score 0. Fixes: stemming/prefix matching, extended Lesk with related synsets' glosses, richer glosses, or embeddings.
mistakes: Assuming a tie means both senses are right.

q: How does embedding-based WSD work?
short: Embed the sentence and each sense's gloss (or example sentences) with an encoder; choose the sense with the highest cosine similarity; with contextual embeddings, compare the target word's contextual vector to sense prototypes.
detail: No labelled data needed for gloss-based variant.
mistakes: Using static word vectors for the target (same for all senses).

q: When is the Naive Bayes independence assumption harmful?
short: When features are strongly correlated (e.g. two features derived from the same underlying data), the model double-counts evidence and becomes overconfident or wrong; bag-of-words context is closer to independent, which is why NB works decently for WSD.
mistakes: Assuming NB is fine for any features.

q: Compare the four WSD families.
short: MFS: no context, strong baseline. Supervised (NB): accurate with labels, expensive data. Embedding similarity: no labels, modern default. Lesk/knowledge-based: needs only a dictionary/graph, brittle exact matching.

q: How do relations differ by part of speech in WordNet?
short: Nouns: hypernymy/hyponymy and meronymy/holonymy. Verbs: hypernymy via troponymy (snore is a manner of sleeping) and entailment (snore → sleep). Adjectives: antonymy and similarity clusters.

q: Build a WSD component for a search engine query expander.
short: Use embedding similarity between the query context and WordNet/encyclopedia glosses, fall back to MFS for one-word queries, use click logs to learn domain sense priors, expand queries only with synonyms of the chosen sense, and evaluate on labelled queries against MFS.
detail: Avoid expanding 'bank' with 'shore' for finance queries.
mistakes: Expanding with all synonyms of all senses.

q: Why is fine-grained WSD hard to evaluate?
short: WordNet senses can be very fine; human annotators agree only moderately at that level, which caps achievable accuracy; coarse-grained sense groups and task-based evaluation are often more meaningful.

q: Do large language models make WSD obsolete?
short: They disambiguate implicitly when translating or answering, so standalone WSD is less often needed; explicit WSD still matters for linking text to lexicons/knowledge graphs, interpretable pipelines, low-resource settings and evaluation of model understanding.
detail: Entity linking is a close cousin.
follow: How to test an LLM's WSD?

q: How can WordNet's hierarchy itself drive disambiguation?
short: Locate each candidate sense in the hierarchy and measure how related the context words' senses are to it (e.g. path or information-content similarity); choose the sense whose neighbourhood best matches the context (bat near cave/wings → mammal branch).

q: Get sense-labelled data cheaply for supervised WSD.
short: Bootstrap with seeds and 'one sense per discourse/collocation' heuristics (Yarowsky), use parallel corpora where translations differ by sense (bank → banque/rive), use encyclopedia links as labels, or have an LLM pre-label for human verification.
